tldr: This is a pattern across six independent arXiv papers, not one event: separate teams keep splitting agent work across cooperating roles. It opened with a multi-agent memory design and a crypto-trading system, then a safety paper argued Codex- and Claude Code-style multi-agent setups fall to attacks single frontier models resist.
whats_new: The latest paper reports a multi-agent system deployed in production to keep customer-facing documentation in sync with fast-moving code.
why_it_matters: Splitting an agent into roles adds new attack surface: the weakest agent sets the safety bar, so per-model red-teaming does not cover the whole system.

beats.headline: Memory and trading papers frame multi-agent as a design pattern
beats.summary: Two unrelated papers use agent roles for long-term memory and for non-stationary market trading.

beats.headline: Attacks that fail on single models break multi-agent systems
beats.summary: A safety paper reports breaks in Codex- and Claude Code-style systems that only appear once work is split across agents.

beats.headline: Role-split agents take on RL training, formal verification, and docs upkeep
beats.summary: Three more independent papers apply the pattern to end-to-end pipelines, one of them deployed.

open_questions: Do Codex or Claude Code ship mitigations for the multi-agent-only break reported on Nov 12?
Does the deployed documentation system publish accuracy or rollback numbers from production?
Do any of these papers report cost or latency against a single-agent baseline?
take_for_builders: If you run sub-agents or orchestrator/worker setups, red-team the composed system end to end, not just each model, and cap what the least-trusted agent can pass downstream.
